title: Startup Survivor: Build a Food Truck Empire
status: Original game-design proposal; not a working game
course: Auburn MBA BUSI 7230 Cost Analysis and Systems, Fall 2026

rounds.title: Buy your first truck
rounds.objective: Differentiate a capitalized asset purchase from an operating expense.
rounds.scenario: The owner invests $25,000 cash. A working truck includes equipment and will be depreciated straight-line over 60 months with zero salvage value. All three options can serve the same menu, but have different monthly capacity.

mastery_check.prompt: With a $12,000 truck, how much cash remains immediately after the purchase?
mastery_check.formula: Cash after purchase = $25,000 - truck purchase price.
mastery_check.feedback_for_wrong_answers: An equipment purchase is not an immediate $12,000 operating expense. It exchanges one asset, cash, for another, equipment. Depreciation allocates the cost over its useful life.

options.label: Used truck - $12,000
options.effect: Dr Equipment 12,000 / Cr Cash 12,000; capacity 1,200 meals/month; monthly depreciation $200, beginning Month 1.

options.label: Refurbished truck - $15,000
options.effect: Dr Equipment 15,000 / Cr Cash 15,000; capacity 1,550 meals/month; monthly depreciation $250.

options.label: Premium truck - $19,000
options.effect: Dr Equipment 19,000 / Cr Cash 19,000; capacity 2,100 meals/month; monthly depreciation $316.67, with final-month rounding catch-up.

rounds.accounting_posting: On purchase: Assets Cash decreases; PPE increases equally; profit unchanged. At each month-end: Dr Depreciation Expense / Cr Accumulated Depreciation.
rounds.designer_notes: The premium option leaves little early liquidity; do not automatically mark it wrong. Ask the student to defend cash-versus-capacity tradeoffs.

rounds.title: Choose where to park and prepare food
rounds.objective: Distinguish fixed rent from a per-order variable service fee and identify an activity-level crossover.
rounds.scenario: Every facility requires an $800 refundable deposit. All leases provide access to a safe, fully permitted operating site. Other baseline cash costs are payroll $3,600, utilities $350, insurance $250, and marketing $200 per month.

mastery_check.prompt: At 1,000 orders, which of these two location contracts costs less: Economy at $900 + $0.50 per order, or Standard at $1,300?
mastery_check.worked_solution: At 1,000 meals, Economy costs $1,400 and Standard costs $1,300; Standard is cheaper by $100.
mastery_check.feedback_for_wrong_answers: At low volumes, the fixed-plus-variable contract may be cheaper. At higher volumes, the flat lease can win. The deposit is an asset, not rent expense.

options.label: Economy site
options.effect: Refundable cash deposit $800 becomes Deposits asset; recurring cash rent $900/month plus variable location fee $0.50 for every fulfilled order; no additional demand.

options.label: Standard site
options.effect: Same $800 deposit; recurring fixed cash rent $1,300/month; no per-order fee; no additional demand.

options.label: High-traffic site
options.effect: Same $800 deposit; recurring fixed cash rent $1,900/month; adds 250 regular prospective orders/month, subject to capacity.

rounds.accounting_posting: Dr Refundable Deposits 800 / Cr Cash 800. Recognize actual rent and economy service fees as monthly expenses when incurred.
rounds.designer_notes: Mastery numeric answer $1,300 tests selection via cheapest cost; UI also shows $1,400 Economy and $800-order crossover.

rounds.title: Price your signature bowl
rounds.objective: Calculate contribution margin and see how price influences both unit economics and demand.
rounds.scenario: Base bowl variable cost is $5: non-sauce ingredients $2.50, sauce $1.30, packaging $0.80, and payment fee $0.40. The below demand estimates are original game assumptions, not external market data.

mastery_check.prompt: At a $12 price and $5 variable cost, what is the contribution margin per bowl?
mastery_check.formula: Unit CM = selling price - unit variable cost; CM ratio = CM / selling price.
mastery_check.feedback_for_wrong_answers: Revenue is not profit. Only the difference between selling price and variable cost contributes to covering fixed costs and operating income.

options.label: Value price - $10
options.effect: Set bowl price $10; regular baseline demand 1,250 bowls/month before capacity, location and promotion effects; base CM $5.

options.label: Balanced price - $12
options.effect: Set bowl price $12; baseline demand 1,100 bowls/month; base CM $7.

options.label: Premium price - $14
options.effect: Set bowl price $14; baseline demand 850 bowls/month; base CM $9.

rounds.accounting_posting: No journal entry on pricing selection. Recognize revenue and variable expenses for actual fulfilled orders at month close.
rounds.designer_notes: No fixed best price: the best choice depends on facility choice, capacity, promotion choices and later cost shocks.

rounds.title: Find your break-even point
rounds.objective: Compute break-even units using recurring fixed expenses, depreciation and all variable per-order costs.
rounds.scenario: A basic launch planning case uses monthly fixed cash costs: payroll $3,600; utilities $350; insurance $250; marketing $200; standard location rent $1,300. Used truck depreciation is $200. Bowl price is $12 and unit variable cost $5.

mastery_check.prompt: How many bowls per month must this business sell to break even on operating profit?
mastery_check.formula: Fixed operating costs = 3600+350+250+200+1300+200=5900; BE units = CEILING(5900/(12-5)).
mastery_check.worked_solution: $5,900 / $7 = 842.857; round UP to 843 bowls. At 842 bowls, operating income is still negative.
mastery_check.feedback_for_wrong_answers: Break-even uses contribution margin, not selling price. Round UP because selling part of a meal is not an option. One-time launch costs should not be silently mixed into a recurring baseline.

options.label: Launch-day publicity
options.effect: One-time marketing cash payment/expense $250 in Month 1; raises Month 1 regular demand by 130 meals, subject to capacity.

options.label: Service-speed workshop
options.effect: One-time training cash payment/expense $180 in Month 1; increases Month 1 capacity by 100 meals; no recurring boost.

options.label: Preserve the cash
options.effect: No change to cost, demand or capacity.

rounds.accounting_posting: At Month 1 close, recognize the one-time marketing/training expense and cash outflow if selected.
rounds.designer_notes: Actual game quiz calculates from the chosen truck, location, price and recurring costs; the $843 example is a fixed instructional reference case.

rounds.title: Set the first operating profit target
rounds.objective: Calculate the units required to achieve a target operating profit and choose a demand-generation budget.
rounds.scenario: Use the same standalone reference case as Round 4: fixed operating costs $5,900/month, bowl CM $7/unit. The owner wants $1,500 monthly operating profit.

mastery_check.prompt: How many bowls are needed to earn $1,500 of operating profit?
mastery_check.formula: Target units = CEILING((fixed operating costs + target profit) / unit contribution margin).
mastery_check.feedback_for_wrong_answers: To reach a specific profit target, fixed costs AND desired profit must be covered by contribution margin. The advertising decision changes both sides of the profit equation.

options.label: Growth-first advertising
options.effect: Add $300 to recurring monthly fixed marketing expense beginning Month 1; add 200 to regular monthly demand from Month 1 onward.

options.label: Moderate advertising
options.effect: Add $150 to recurring fixed marketing beginning Month 1; add 120 to regular demand from Month 1 onward.

options.label: Operate lean
options.effect: No extra fixed marketing and no extra demand; preserve liquidity.

rounds.accounting_posting: Marketing is expensed monthly when services are received and paid. Its expected demand benefit does not create an asset or revenue until sales occur.
rounds.designer_notes: Checkpoint 1: display opening cash, truck capacity, unit CM, planned break-even, intended target units and one-sentence learning summary.

rounds.title: Add a second menu item
rounds.objective: Use a weighted-average contribution margin for a multi-product business.
rounds.scenario: A wrap sells for $10 and costs $4.50 per unit: non-sauce ingredients $2, sauce $1.30, packaging $0.80 and payment $0.40. Bowls sell for $12 with $5 variable cost in the reference case.

mastery_check.prompt: With a mix of 75% bowls and 25% wraps, what is the weighted-average contribution margin per meal?
mastery_check.formula: WACM = bowl mix * ($12-$5) + wrap mix * ($10-$4.50).
mastery_check.worked_solution: 0.75*$7 + 0.25*$5.50 = $6.625 per meal (display $6.63; retain full precision internally).
mastery_check.feedback_for_wrong_answers: A greater number of sales does not always mean more profit. Use weighted contribution margin and account for the added recurring menu-support cost.

options.label: Lean two-item menu
options.effect: Keep a simple menu with 90% bowls and 10% wraps; no complexity fee or new demand.

options.label: Balanced menu
options.effect: 25% of regular monthly orders are wraps; new monthly regular demand +100 orders; recurring cash menu-support cost $120/month.

options.label: Wrap-forward menu
options.effect: 45% of regular monthly orders are wraps; new monthly demand +180 orders; recurring cash menu-support cost $200/month.

rounds.accounting_posting: All sales and associated actual variable expenses are recognized only when orders are fulfilled; recurring menu support is included in fixed monthly cash operating expense.
rounds.designer_notes: To avoid fraction-of-a-meal errors, allocate whole units via largest-remainder rounding; bowl + wrap units must equal the regular-orders total.

rounds.title: Should you join a delivery platform?
rounds.objective: Evaluate a new sales channel based on incremental contribution and available capacity.
rounds.scenario: A delivery app expects 180 additional bowl orders/month. It charges 25% of the bowl selling price per app order. A direct-order campaign offers 100 extra orders/month but costs $150/month.

mastery_check.prompt: For a $12 bowl with $5 variable costs and a 25% app commission, what is contribution margin on ONE app order?
mastery_check.formula: App-order CM = bowl price - bowl unit cost - app commission rate * bowl price.
mastery_check.worked_solution: $12 - $5 - (0.25*$12) = $4 per delivery order.
mastery_check.feedback_for_wrong_answers: App sales may look attractive in revenue terms but only the contribution AFTER the app fee covers fixed costs. At capacity, new channel orders may displace more profitable walk-in sales.

options.label: Join the app
options.effect: Add a distinct app-order channel with 180 monthly bowl orders; app fee 25% of collected selling price per fulfilled app order; no new fixed fee.

options.label: Promote direct online orders
options.effect: Add distinct direct-pickup channel with 100 monthly bowl orders; add recurring marketing cash cost $150/month; no commission.

options.label: Stick to walk-up orders
options.effect: No channel cost and no added channel demand.

rounds.accounting_posting: At month close post actual channel gross sales as Revenue, app percentage as selling expense, direct per-order costs as variable expense, and fixed direct marketing separately.
rounds.designer_notes: Channel demand is not guaranteed fulfilled sales; a documented capacity allocator must avoid counting demand exceeding the truck's capacity.

rounds.title: Run a discount promotion
rounds.objective: Evaluate how a discount applied to existing customers can destroy margin even when it increases unit sales.
rounds.scenario: An illustrative test has 1,100 full-price bowl orders at $12 price and $5 unit cost. A blanket $1 discount brings 200 new meals, but also reduces the price of all 1,100 orders that would have purchased anyway.

mastery_check.prompt: Without a capacity limit, what is the incremental contribution from the blanket $1 discount?
mastery_check.formula: Delta CM = new orders*(discounted price - variable cost) - existing orders*discount amount.
mastery_check.worked_solution: 200*($11-$5) - 1,100*$1 = $1,200 - $1,100 = +$100, before any extra marketing expense.
mastery_check.feedback_for_wrong_answers: The blanket promotion gives a price reduction to existing customers too. Its financial outcome may turn negative once real capacity constraints are applied.

options.label: Discount ALL walk-up orders by $1
options.effect: In Month 1 only, subtract $1 from selling price of every regular bowl/wrap order, and add 200 potential regular orders before capacity allocation.

options.label: Target new customers only
options.effect: In Month 1 only, spend $100 marketing; add 120 distinct coupon-only bowl orders priced at bowl price minus $1; existing orders retain full price.

options.label: No promotion
options.effect: No discount, marketing or new promotional demand.

rounds.accounting_posting: Discounts reduce transaction revenue; the $100 targeted campaign is separately expensed. Store eligible channel and price for each order cohort.
rounds.designer_notes: Never calculate discount gains using only incremental units. Include margin lost on customers who were already buying.

rounds.title: Increase service capacity
rounds.objective: Compare added fixed hiring expense with variable overtime to relieve a capacity bottleneck.
rounds.scenario: A used truck normally serves 1,200 orders/month. For an isolated 120-order overflow at $7 regular CM, a part-time employee costs $650/month and overtime costs $2 for each order served above base capacity.

mastery_check.prompt: If all 120 overflow orders can be served, what is the ONE-MONTH incremental operating profit from overtime?
mastery_check.formula: Overtime delta profit = overflow units * (ordinary unit CM - extra overtime cost per unit).
mastery_check.worked_solution: 120*($7-$2) = $600 incremental operating profit for the month.
mastery_check.feedback_for_wrong_answers: Labor is neither always fixed nor always variable. Hiring can be a step-fixed cost, while overtime can add variable cost only to units produced beyond normal capacity.

options.label: Hire a part-time employee
options.effect: Increase capacity +300 meals/month from this month onward; recurring cash payroll expense +$650/month.

options.label: Use overtime this month
options.effect: Increase capacity +180 meals for Month 1 only; charge an extra $2 variable overtime for each fulfilled meal above the pre-R9 capacity threshold, maximum 180.

options.label: Keep the current crew
options.effect: No capacity or expense change; potential orders above capacity are unfilled.

rounds.accounting_posting: Recognize part-time pay in monthly payroll or temporary overtime expense based on actual overflow fulfilled. No salaries are capitalized.
rounds.designer_notes: Keep a separate base-capacity threshold so overtime is not incorrectly charged on every meal sold.

rounds.title: Win a catering contract
rounds.objective: Evaluate a special order using incremental revenues, relevant costs, and displaced ordinary sales.
rounds.scenario: A client offers a one-time Month 1 event. Each catered bowl costs the ordinary bowl variable cost ($5 in the reference case) plus $1 extra event packaging/transport. Event setup is $180.

mastery_check.prompt: Ignoring capacity constraints, what is the incremental profit from 140 catered bowls sold at $11 each?
mastery_check.formula: Catering contribution - setup = Q*(event price - (bowl variable cost + $1)) - setup fee.
mastery_check.worked_solution: 140*($11-$6)-$180 = $520 incremental operating profit, before displaced regular business.
mastery_check.feedback_for_wrong_answers: The $520 result is true only IF the new order does not displace more profitable customers. Opportunity cost = contribution lost on displaced orders; subtract it from incremental catering profit.

options.label: Accept all 220 meals at $9
options.effect: Contract 220 bowls for $9 each; variable cost = live bowl cost + $1 per meal; one-time $180 setup expense; event orders receive first capacity priority.

options.label: Negotiate 140 meals at $11
options.effect: Contract 140 bowls for $11 each; variable cost = live bowl cost + $1 per meal; same $180 setup; event orders receive first capacity priority.

options.label: Decline the contract
options.effect: No catering sales or setup expense; preserve capacity for regular and delivery customers.

rounds.accounting_posting: Catering cash received upon service. Recognize revenue and related direct costs in Month 1; setup is a period expense. Close Month 1 and generate the first operating income statement.
rounds.designer_notes: Close Month 1 after this round. The standard fulfillment order is catering contract -> walk-up regular -> direct pickup/coupons -> app delivery, always subject to capacity. Revenue is based on served, not desired, meals.

rounds.title: Ingredient prices jump
rounds.objective: Analyze a commodity-cost increase and decide whether to absorb, pass on, or reduce the increase.
rounds.scenario: A supplier shock adds $0.60 of non-sauce ingredient cost per meal. A replacement supplier would limit the increase to $0.20 but charges a $240 onboarding fee. Price increases of $1 reduce prospective price-sensitive demand by 8% (game assumption).

mastery_check.prompt: If 1,000 meals are sold and the business absorbs the full cost increase, how much does operating contribution decline?
mastery_check.formula: Change in total variable costs = actual meals * added variable cost per meal.
mastery_check.worked_solution: 1,000*$0.60 = $600 decrease in monthly contribution, all else equal.
mastery_check.feedback_for_wrong_answers: A price increase may restore unit CM but lose customers. Compare total expected contribution at realistic demand rather than assuming passing on cost is always best.

options.label: Absorb the entire increase
options.effect: Permanently add $0.60 to non-sauce ingredients per fulfilled meal beginning Month 2; no price or demand change.

options.label: Raise every current menu price by $1
options.effect: Permanently add $0.60 non-sauce cost per meal AND raise currently offered bowl/wrap prices by $1; multiply future price-sensitive demand by 0.92. The later premium price is set explicitly in Round 14.

options.label: Switch ingredient suppliers
options.effect: Permanently add only $0.20 non-sauce cost per meal; expense/pay $240 one-time onboarding in Month 2; no menu price or demand change.

rounds.accounting_posting: Ingredient surcharge is variable food cost as sold; onboarding fee is a one-time period expense when incurred and paid.
rounds.designer_notes: Do not apply the $0.60 shock first and then add an additional $0.20 for the switch. Selected post-shock surcharge is $0.20 total.

rounds.title: Make your own sauce?
rounds.objective: Distinguish relevant make-or-buy costs from capital expenditures and depreciation.
rounds.scenario: Each meal uses one portion of sauce that currently costs $1.30 from the supplier. You could produce sauce for $0.80 per portion, incur $90 additional monthly fixed kitchen labor, and buy a $180 mixer depreciated over 60 months. A bulk vendor offers $1.05 per portion with a $200 one-time onboarding fee.

mastery_check.prompt: Ignoring the $180 initial cash purchase, at how many portions does making sauce break even on MONTHLY operating income (including $3 monthly depreciation)?
mastery_check.formula: Make operating advantage per portion = $1.30 - $0.80 = $0.50; incremental monthly fixed cost = $90 + $180/60 = $93.
mastery_check.worked_solution: $93 / $0.50 = 186 portions/month. Cash operating break-even would be 180, before considering the one-time $180 investment.
mastery_check.feedback_for_wrong_answers: Do not expense the full mixer purchase immediately. $90 fixed labor changes profit today; $180 is upfront cash and an equipment asset, allocated through depreciation over time.

options.label: Continue buying sauce
options.effect: Keep sauce component at $1.30 per fulfilled meal; no fixed cost or capital purchase.

options.label: Make sauce in-house
options.effect: Set sauce component to $0.80 per meal; recurring incremental cash fixed kitchen labor $90/month starting Month 2; purchase mixer $180 PPE, 60-month zero-salvage life, $3/month depreciation.

options.label: Negotiate bulk vendor pricing
options.effect: Set sauce component to $1.05 per meal from Month 2; expense/pay a one-time $200 vendor onboarding fee; no extra monthly fixed cost.

rounds.accounting_posting: For a mixer purchase post Dr PPE/Cr Cash; depreciate $3/month from its service month. Sauce cost flows through variable food expense on meals actually sold.
rounds.designer_notes: Savings are per *all fulfilled meals*, including wrap, premium, delivery, and catering, except R21's separate corporate order is priced as an all-in case.

rounds.title: Find hidden product costs
rounds.objective: Allocate existing overhead by appropriate activity drivers without confusing allocated cost with incremental cash cost.
rounds.scenario: For a self-contained ABC lesson, $1,200 of existing monthly support cost relates to 60 prep batches and $900 of existing support cost to 450 support contacts. Wraps use 1 prep batch per 25 wraps and 0.4 support contacts per wrap.

mastery_check.prompt: What is the ABC overhead assigned to one wrap?
mastery_check.formula: Batch rate = 1200/60 = $20 per batch; contact rate = 900/450 = $2 per contact; per-wrap ABC = (1/25)*20 + 0.4*2.
mastery_check.worked_solution: $0.80 batch support + $0.80 customer support = $1.60 allocated overhead per wrap.
mastery_check.feedback_for_wrong_answers: The $1.60 is a cost allocation, not necessarily an avoidable cash expense from selling one more wrap. Do NOT add the $2,100 cost pools on top of the operating expenses already in the ledger.

options.label: Promote bowls
options.effect: Spend/expense $100 once in Month 2; add 50 potential bowl orders in Month 2 only.

options.label: Promote wraps
options.effect: Spend/expense $100 once in Month 2; add 70 potential wrap orders in Month 2 only (only if wraps were added in Round 6).

options.label: No extra promotion
options.effect: Leave the menu mix and monthly demand unchanged; calculate allocations for informational reporting only.

rounds.accounting_posting: ABC allocation is managerial-reporting-only. Only actual $100 marketing choices have cash/P&L effects. Total company expense must be identical before and after a pure reallocation.
rounds.designer_notes: Every player offers at least 10% wraps after Round 6, so all ABC and segment options remain meaningful.

rounds.title: Launch a premium menu item
rounds.objective: Account for cannibalization and the incremental costs of a new menu item.
rounds.scenario: A gourmet bowl costs $7 variable per unit before supplier/sauce modifiers. A $16 version is forecast to attract 180 orders but replaces 70 regular bowls; a $14 version is forecast to attract 260 orders but replaces 150 regular bowls. Either launch incurs $250 one-time design/advertising.

mastery_check.prompt: At ordinary bowl CM $7, what is the incremental contribution of the $16 premium launch after its $250 setup, before capacity effects?
mastery_check.formula: Incremental = premium Q*(premium price-premium variable cost) - displaced ordinary Q*ordinary bowl CM - setup.
mastery_check.feedback_for_wrong_answers: A new product can appear more profitable than it actually is if part of its demand comes from customers who would otherwise buy the standard menu.

options.label: Launch $16 gourmet bowl
options.effect: Add premium cohort with 180 monthly potential orders, price $16, baseline unit variable cost $7 plus live ingredient modifications; remove 70 potential regular bowls/month; expense/pay $250 launch cost in Month 2.

options.label: Launch $14 value gourmet bowl
options.effect: Add premium cohort with 260 monthly potential orders, price $14, baseline unit variable cost $7 plus modifications; remove 150 potential regular bowls/month; expense/pay $250 launch cost in Month 2.

options.label: Delay premium launch
options.effect: No premium orders or launch expense; preserve existing menu.

rounds.accounting_posting: Only fulfilled premium orders create revenue/variable expense. One-time launch campaign is expensed. Apply constrained-capacity allocation before determining realized gain.
rounds.designer_notes: The teaching case uses pre-shock baseline costs; the live game must incorporate Round 11 and 12 cost decisions when forecasting this investment.

rounds.title: Approve next month's operating budget
rounds.objective: Translate unit forecasts into a contribution-format operating budget and fund a management initiative.
rounds.scenario: A reference monthly budget calls for 1,100 standard bowls at $12, variable cost $5/meal, and $5,900 fixed operating expense.

mastery_check.prompt: What is budgeted operating income in the reference case?
mastery_check.formula: Budgeted income = budgeted units*(price - variable unit cost) - budgeted fixed operating costs.
mastery_check.feedback_for_wrong_answers: The budget is a PLAN, not actual revenue. After this choice, let the player lock a Month 3 forecast and show expected operating income; unexpected Month 3 events arrive next chapter.

options.label: Fund new advertising
options.effect: Beginning Month 3, raise fixed cash advertising $200/month and forecast +130 potential regular orders/month.

options.label: Fund food-waste training
options.effect: Pay/expense $400 at the start of Month 3; halves the upcoming baseline waste surcharge in Round 17 from $0.20 to $0.10 per meal.

options.label: Hold cash reserves
options.effect: No additional planned expenditure or demand; keep costs steady.

rounds.accounting_posting: At Round 15 close recognize Month 2 actual results only. The Month 3 initiative is scheduled and posted in Month 3, then the Month 3 static budget is frozen before demand shock.
rounds.designer_notes: Checkpoint 3: include budget vs Month 2 actual, and freeze Month 3 planned units, mix, price, standards and fixed costs for variance analysis.

rounds.title: Sales slump!
rounds.objective: Separate lower activity volume from spending and pricing performance.
rounds.scenario: A bad-weather episode reduces Month 3 price-sensitive walk-up demand by 12%. An instructional budget expected 1,100 meals, $7 contribution per meal; actual demand from the 12% reduction is 968 meals.

mastery_check.prompt: What is the sales-volume CONTRIBUTION variance (actual minus budgeted) in this example?
mastery_check.formula: Sales-volume contribution variance = (actual units - budgeted units) * budgeted unit contribution margin.
mastery_check.worked_solution: (968-1,100)*$7 = -$924, a $924 unfavorable volume variance.
mastery_check.feedback_for_wrong_answers: A sales-volume variance is not the same thing as a material price variance or an unfavorable spending variance. Show the counterfactual results at the original planned activity level.

options.label: Shorten crew shifts temporarily
options.effect: Reduce Month 3 cash payroll/fixed expense by $400; reduce Month 3 capacity by 100 units; restore both in Month 4.

options.label: Emergency promotion
options.effect: Spend/expense $200 only in Month 3; recover 140 potential regular meals in Month 3, subject to capacity.

options.label: Ride out the weather
options.effect: No new cost or demand response; actual activity stays depressed for Month 3 only.

rounds.accounting_posting: Reduce only Month 3 demand, not all months. Apply temporary changes once and reverse before Month 4.
rounds.designer_notes: Use the player's frozen budget standards for live variances; the 1,100-to-968 instructional example remains fixed for standardized mastery checking.

rounds.title: Food waste and material variances
rounds.objective: Calculate the materials price and usage variances and diagnose causes separately.
rounds.scenario: A standalone audit finds 900 meals made. Standard recipe: 2.0 ingredient units/meal at $1.50/unit. Actual consumption: 1,980 ingredient units at $1.65/unit. The live business also faces a small Month 3 waste surcharge of $0.20 per fulfilled meal (or $0.10 if it trained in Round 15).

mastery_check.prompt: What is the TOTAL unfavorable direct-materials variance in the audit?
mastery_check.formula: APV = (actual price - standard price)*actual quantity; AUV = (actual quantity - allowed standard quantity)*standard price.
mastery_check.feedback_for_wrong_answers: Unfavorable price variance and unfavorable quantity variance have different causes. Keep standard quantity at actual output, not original budgeted output.

options.label: Train food-prep employees
options.effect: Spend/expense $180 once in Month 3; final waste cost surcharge becomes $0.05 per fulfilled meal for Month 3 onward.

options.label: Renegotiate ingredient pricing
options.effect: Spend/expense $200 once in Month 3; reduce non-sauce ingredient cost by $0.15 per meal from Month 3 onward; waste surcharge stays at $0.20 (or $0.10 if pre-trained).

options.label: Do nothing
options.effect: Leave waste surcharge at $0.20/meal in Month 3 onward (or $0.10 if trained in Round 15); no new expense.

rounds.accounting_posting: Live waste surcharges are added to actual variable ingredient cost; separate cash action fees are expensed. The fixed teaching case does not automatically inject an additional $567 into the live ledger.
rounds.designer_notes: The optional ingredient renegotiation applies once; it does not cancel a separate supplier surcharge without being recorded explicitly.

rounds.title: A labor-efficiency problem
rounds.objective: Calculate direct-labor rate and efficiency variances using ACTUAL hours and standard hours for actual output.
rounds.scenario: In a projected Month 3 staffing unit, standard labor is 180 hours at $20/hour ($3,600 budget). Without action, expected actual labor is 198 hours at $22/hour ($4,356), an incremental variance of $756 above baseline planned wages. You can intervene before the shift.

mastery_check.prompt: What is the total unfavorable labor variance for the projected shift?
mastery_check.formula: Rate = (AR-SR)*AH; Efficiency=(AH-SH)*SR; sum = AH*AR - SH*SR.
mastery_check.feedback_for_wrong_answers: Rate variance uses ACTUAL hours, not standard hours. The standard $3,600 wage bill is already part of baseline recurring payroll, so only the excess and interventions are incremental in the live month.

options.label: Targeted shift coaching
options.effect: Pay/expense $220 once in Month 3; projected excess payroll above baseline falls from $756 to $456; total incremental cash operating cost $676.

options.label: Bring in an experienced floater
options.effect: Pay/expense $350 once in Month 3; projected excess payroll falls from $756 to $256; total incremental expense/cash cost $606.

options.label: Absorb the overtime
options.effect: Excess actual payroll is $756 above planned payroll; no intervention fee.

rounds.accounting_posting: At Month 3 close, expense the chosen excess payroll and one-time intervention. Cash payments equal recognized labor and intervention expenses.
rounds.designer_notes: Do not first book the full $756 and then also book the reduced $456/$256 excess; use the selected projected outcome only.

rounds.title: Explain the monthly variances
rounds.modules: 22: static vs flexible budgets; 23: responsibility reports
rounds.objective: Reconcile static-budget, flexible-budget and actual performance without attributing volume changes to cost managers.
rounds.scenario: A reference budget for 1,000 meals at $12 price, $5 variable cost and $5,900 fixed overhead yields $1,100 operating income. Actual activity was 900 meals; a properly flexed budget gives $400. Suppose actual income is $250.

mastery_check.prompt: What is the $-amount of the UNFAVORABLE flexible-budget operating-income variance (actual minus flexible budget)?
mastery_check.formula: Flexible budget income at actual volume = 900*($12-$5)-5900=400; flexible-budget variance = actual operating income - flexible budget income.
mastery_check.worked_solution: $250 - $400 = -$150, or $150 unfavorable. The separate sales-volume variance is $400-$1,100 = -$700.
mastery_check.feedback_for_wrong_answers: A decline in total profit from lower volume does not necessarily indicate poor spending control. Flexible budgets hold activity constant to compare the cost side properly.

options.label: Investigate the cost drivers
options.effect: No immediate financial change; earn an analysis achievement if the student explains both the $700 volume variance and $150 flex variance.

options.label: Cut marketing permanently
options.effect: Beginning Month 4, decrease recurring marketing cash expense by $150/month; reduce future regular demand by 120 meals/month.

options.label: Raise menu prices
options.effect: Beginning Month 4, add $1 to bowl and wrap selling prices (and premium if active); reduce price-sensitive demand by 8%.

rounds.accounting_posting: The fixed illustrative variance exercise is separate from the player's live variance report, which must use actual budget snapshots and fulfilled output.
rounds.designer_notes: Never penalize an operations manager for a 12% weather-driven sales decline in the controllable-cost score.

rounds.title: Drop the low-profit wrap?
rounds.objective: Avoid dropping a profitable segment merely because allocated common fixed costs make reported segment income negative.
rounds.scenario: A reference wrap segment sells 400 wraps at $10 each with $4.50 variable cost per wrap, direct avoidable fixed costs of $300, and allocated common overhead of $2,200. The overhead would continue if the segment were dropped.

mastery_check.prompt: How much total COMPANY operating profit is LOST by dropping wraps, assuming no replacement sales?
mastery_check.formula: Lost segment margin = segment revenue - segment variable costs - avoidable fixed costs. Common allocated cost is irrelevant if unavoidable.
mastery_check.worked_solution: 400*($10-$4.50)-$300 = $2,200-$300=$1,900 decrease in company operating income if dropped.
mastery_check.feedback_for_wrong_answers: An allocated segment loss is not sufficient evidence to discontinue. Use contribution that would be lost minus costs actually avoided, and account for any replacement sales.

options.label: Keep the wrap line
options.effect: Retain the selected wrap share, menu-support fixed cost and demand from Round 6.

options.label: Discontinue wraps
options.effect: From Month 4 onward, remove wrap orders/demand and any separately modeled avoidable recurring wrap-support fee; add 100 prospective replacement bowl orders/month; leave common shared overhead unchanged.

options.label: Redesign the wrap recipe
options.effect: Spend/expense $180 once in Month 4; lower variable wrap cost $0.60 per sold wrap, reduce wrap demand by 7% from Month 4 onward.

rounds.accounting_posting: At month close post actual sales and variable expenses; after Round 20 restore Month 3 temporary weather/overtime effects before Month 4.
rounds.designer_notes: If wraps are discontinued, remove the +100/+180 menu-driven demand boost from R6, turn wrap share to zero, reverse avoidable wrap-support fee, and add only the 100 specified replacement bowl prospects. Common overhead continues.

rounds.title: Profitable... but short on cash
rounds.objective: Reconcile cash and accrual profit, record accounts receivable, and evaluate early collection discounts.
rounds.scenario: A one-time Month 4 corporate order has already been delivered using offsite capacity. Invoice price is $2,400, and all-in direct production costs paid now are $1,000. The client normally pays after Month 4. Alternatives provide immediate collection.

mastery_check.prompt: If the client does NOT pay by month-end, how much operating profit is earned from this invoice BEFORE other overheads?
mastery_check.formula: Accrual gross contribution = revenue earned - production expense incurred, regardless of collection.
mastery_check.worked_solution: $2,400 revenue - $1,000 cash-paid production cost = $1,400 profit contribution; A/R increases $2,400 while cash decreases $1,000.
mastery_check.feedback_for_wrong_answers: Net income and cash can move differently. A completed sale on credit creates revenue and receivable even though the bank account is still waiting.

options.label: Invoice at normal terms
options.effect: Dr A/R 2,400 / Cr Sales 2,400; pay/expense $1,000 direct production; invoice remains outstanding at Month 4 end; cash received only in future period.

options.label: Offer 2% early-payment discount
options.effect: Collect $2,352 immediately; journal: Dr Cash 2,352; Dr Sales Discounts (contra-revenue) 48; Cr Sales Revenue 2,400. Recognize net sales of $2,352 and $1,000 direct production expense. No ending A/R for this invoice.

options.label: Factor the invoice without recourse
options.effect: Recognize $2,400 sales and $1,000 cost; transfer $2,400 A/R to a factor for $2,304 cash, expense $96 factoring fee; no ending A/R.

rounds.accounting_posting: The invoice is a completed service outside the truck capacity model; the $1,000 is an incremental period variable expense, paid once. Never book it a second time at month close.
rounds.designer_notes: Offer the early-discount choice as an explicit 2% reduction in revenue, not as an unexplained reduction in A/R.

rounds.title: The refrigerator breaks
rounds.objective: Classify a routine repair separately from purchasing an upgraded long-lived asset.
rounds.scenario: Your existing refrigerator can be repaired for $650. Alternatively, install an additional upgraded $1,800 refrigeration system with a 36-month zero-residual life that saves $0.18 in spoilage per meal. Or rent a temporary equivalent refrigerator for $130 for Month 4.

mastery_check.prompt: If the new refrigerator costs $1,800 and lasts 36 months with no residual value, what is monthly straight-line depreciation?
mastery_check.formula: Monthly depreciation = (capitalized cost - residual value) / useful months.
mastery_check.feedback_for_wrong_answers: Capitalizing ordinary repairs would overstate current profit. Buying a distinct multi-year asset does not make $1,800 an immediate operating expense.

options.label: Repair existing refrigerator
options.effect: Cash -$650, Repairs Expense +$650 in Month 4; restore normal operating capacity; no new fixed asset.

options.label: Install upgraded refrigeration
options.effect: Cash -$1,800, PPE +$1,800; depreciate $50 from Month 4; reduce spoilage variable cost by $0.18 per actual sold meal from Month 4 onward.

options.label: Rent a temporary unit
options.effect: Expense/pay $130 in Month 4 for temporary rental; capacity restored for the month; no new asset or savings in per-meal cost.

rounds.accounting_posting: Classify the purchase in PPE; depreciation reduces income but is noncash. Old truck assets remain in service; the game assumes no asset disposal or impairment.
rounds.designer_notes: Every option maintains food safety and service capacity; the educational choice is cost classification and expected economics, not food safety.

rounds.title: Invest in faster preparation equipment
rounds.objective: Evaluate a capital purchase using future incremental cash flows and differentiate NPV from accounting profit.
rounds.scenario: A process improvement machine costs $2,400 today; it saves $1,050 CASH annually in operating costs for 3 years and can be sold for $300 at the end of Year 3. The required return is 10%. Salvage value for depreciation is also assumed $300. Alternative lease is $95/month for the same monthly $87.50 savings.

mastery_check.prompt: What is the project net present value (NPV), rounded to the nearest dollar?
mastery_check.worked_solution: PV yearly savings = $2,611.20; PV terminal value = $225.39; NPV = +$436.59, rounded +$437. Simple payback ignoring residual is 2.29 years.
mastery_check.feedback_for_wrong_answers: Use incremental future CASH flows for NPV; do not subtract depreciation from NPV cash flows. The $300 end-of-life residual occurs in Year 3, not each year.

options.label: Buy the machine
options.effect: Buy $2,400 PPE now; record $300 residual value and depreciation ($2,400-$300)/36=$58.33/month from Month 4; save $87.50 monthly cash operating expense during modeled months.

options.label: Month-to-month equipment rental
options.effect: Take a cancellable month-to-month equipment rental for $95 cash/expense in Month 4, and realize $87.50 monthly operating cash cost savings; the simplified contract does not transfer title and creates no long-term committed lease.

options.label: Keep the existing process
options.effect: No investment or added cash savings.

rounds.accounting_posting: Month 4: post machine acquisition (if bought), month-4 depreciation ($58.33), the $87.50 cost savings, or cancellable monthly rental cost ($95) if rented. Close all Month 4 operating transactions once at this checkpoint before Round 24.
rounds.designer_notes: Close Month 4 after this round, before expansion planning. In actual accounting, non-cancellable leases may require right-of-use assets and liabilities under ASC 842; this option is specifically a cancellable short-term rental. The $300 residual cash comes at Year 3.

rounds.title: Should you open a second truck?
rounds.objective: Calculate a project NPV independently from its financing method, and recognize loan proceeds as liabilities.
rounds.scenario: A second truck costs $18,000 now. It is forecast to generate $6,500 of incremental UNLEVERED cash flow at each of the next four year-ends, plus $3,000 terminal resale cash at Year 4. Hurdle rate: 12%. A bank will finance 60% at 9% APR with 60 equal monthly payments beginning next month.

mastery_check.prompt: What is the NPV of opening the second truck, rounded to the nearest dollar?
mastery_check.feedback_for_wrong_answers: Financing affects liquidity and debt service, not the NPV of the unlevered project. Loan proceeds are not revenue. The same project NPV applies whether paid in cash or financed.

options.label: Buy the second truck with cash
options.effect: After Month 4 close, at the beginning of Month 5: if current cash >= $20,000, purchase the $18,000 truck as PPE for cash; maintain a $2,000 minimum cash reserve. No new-truck Month 4 revenue or depreciation. Depreciate over 48 months with $3,000 salvage from Month 5 if future statements are shown.

options.label: Finance 60% of the truck
options.effect: After Month 4 close, at the beginning of Month 5: if cash >= $9,200, record PPE +$18,000, bank loan +$10,800, cash -$7,200; monthly payment ~$224.19 begins one month later. No new-truck Month 4 revenue/depreciation. $2,000 reserve required.

options.label: Wait and build cash
options.effect: Do not expand; preserve cash, debt capacity and equipment flexibility.

rounds.accounting_posting: At acquisition, Dr PPE 18,000, Cr Cash 18,000 for cash route; financed route also Dr Cash 10,800 / Cr Loan 10,800. Interest begins after month-end. No future projections are falsely counted as current realized profits.
rounds.designer_notes: Round 23 has already closed Month 4. Finance and ownership decisions are start-of-Month-5 transactions and do not retroactively change Month 4 results. Financing affects liquidity/debt service, not project unlevered NPV.
rounds.timing: Start of Month 5, after Month 4 close

rounds.title: Present to the investor committee
rounds.objective: Read the completed financial statements, explain economic tradeoffs, and separate owner distributions, loan payments and prepaid costs from current operating profit.
rounds.scenario: Investors want a reconciled Month 4 income statement, a current balance sheet, a cash-flow bridge, a dashboard of margins, and a one-paragraph recommendation supported by accounting data.

mastery_check.prompt: A business has $12,000 of assets and $4,000 of liabilities. What is book equity?
mastery_check.formula: Assets = Liabilities + Equity; Equity = Assets - Liabilities.
mastery_check.worked_solution: $12,000-$4,000=$8,000 book equity. An owner draw reduces cash and equity, not operating expense.
mastery_check.feedback_for_wrong_answers: Book equity and cash are not synonyms, and an owner distribution does not decrease income. Current-period advertising expense also does not arise merely from paying in advance for next month.

options.label: Distribute $1,000 to owner
options.effect: If cash remains >=$2,000, post a $1,000 owner distribution: Dr Owner Distributions (contra-equity)/Cr Cash; current profit unchanged.

options.label: Retain all current cash
options.effect: No ledger change; show ability to fund payroll, equipment maintenance and future opportunities.

options.label: Prepay $1,000 of next month's advertising
options.effect: If cash remains >=$2,000, Dr Prepaid Advertising 1,000 / Cr Cash 1,000; not expensed until campaign is delivered next month.

rounds.accounting_posting: Generate final 4-month P&L and cash-flow bridge from already-closed months. Update post-Month-4 balance sheet for any R24 capital purchase/loan and R25 distributions or prepayments; do not close Month 4 a second time.
rounds.designer_notes: A post-close owner distribution reduces equity and cash, not Month 4 net income. Any prepaid Month 5 advertising is a current asset until consumed. Provide a restart and copyable report; do not collect personal information.
rounds.timing: Start of Month 5, after Month 4 close

bonus_challenges.title: Allocate overhead by preparation hours
bonus_challenges.scenario: Existing shared monthly overhead is $1,800; bowls use 75 setup/prep hours and wraps use 25 hours.

mastery_check.prompt: How much overhead should the wraps receive if prep hours are the driver?
mastery_check.formula: Rate = 1800/(75+25)=$18/hour; wraps overhead=25*$18.
mastery_check.worked_solution: $450 wraps; $1,350 bowls; total reconciles to $1,800.

options.label: Use preparation hours
options.effect: Correct driver for the stated labor-preparation workload; managerial allocation only.

options.label: Split overhead equally
options.effect: Assign $900 to each line, despite different driver use; demonstrate distortion.

options.label: Allocate by sales revenue
options.effect: Allocate proportionally to revenue; results differ from the specified prep-hour basis.

bonus_challenges.feedback_for_wrong_answers: Allocation redistributes an existing total; it does not create another $1,800 of expense.

bonus_challenges.title: One more employee at a step-cost threshold
bonus_challenges.scenario: You can serve 900 meals; demand is 950. Incremental 50 meals have $7 contribution margin each, but adding a shift costs $400.

mastery_check.prompt: What is the incremental MONTHLY profit from hiring just for these 50 sales?
mastery_check.worked_solution: -$50: reject the $400 shift on these facts unless benefits outside this month justify it.

options.label: Hire additional shift
options.effect: Serve 50 extra, $350 contribution, $400 cost, net -$50.

options.label: Decline the extra 50
options.effect: No additional contribution and no shift cost; profit $50 higher than A.

options.label: Improve kitchen throughput
options.effect: Hypothetical alternative: spend $200 for a one-time 50-meal efficiency boost; net +$150, if feasible.

bonus_challenges.feedback_for_wrong_answers: The most sales is not automatically the most profit; thresholds matter.

bonus_challenges.title: Inventory is not automatically expensed
bonus_challenges.scenario: The owner buys $1,000 ingredients before operating; $720 is used in meals sold, and $280 remains usable in inventory.

mastery_check.prompt: What is closing inventory?
mastery_check.formula: Closing inventory=beginning inventory + purchases - ingredients consumed.
mastery_check.worked_solution: 0+1000-720=$280 inventory; $720 COGS; total cash spend $1,000.

options.label: Record $280 closing inventory
options.effect: Correct: recognize $720 expense and $280 asset.

options.label: Expense all $1,000 now
options.effect: Incorrect: understates inventory and profit by $280.

options.label: Record $1,000 ending inventory
options.effect: Incorrect: ignores $720 ingredients consumed in sold meals.

bonus_challenges.feedback_for_wrong_answers: Cash outflows for buying inventory and expense recognition for ingredients used occur at different points.

bonus_challenges.title: Evaluate managers fairly
bonus_challenges.scenario: A kitchen manager can influence food waste and shift schedules, but cannot control a citywide power rate increase or an unexpected storm.

mastery_check.prompt: How much of a $500 storm-driven sales shortfall is controllable by the kitchen manager without additional evidence?
mastery_check.formula: Responsibility reports should isolate controllable items when evaluating the manager.
mastery_check.worked_solution: $0 directly attributable as a controllable operating cost on the stated evidence.

options.label: Focus on controllable waste and productivity
options.effect: Correct: assess manager using relevant controllable measures.

options.label: Penalize manager for the storm
options.effect: Misattributes demand shock to a production supervisor.

options.label: Ignore all performance measures
options.effect: Fails to use useful operational data, even for controllable costs.

bonus_challenges.feedback_for_wrong_answers: Responsibility accounting is about decision rights and controllability, not only arithmetic.

bonus_challenges.title: Stress-test the second truck
bonus_challenges.scenario: Second-truck cash inflows decline 15%, from $6,500 to $5,525 per year for 4 years. Project remains $18,000 initial investment, $3,000 Year-4 resale and 12% discount.

mastery_check.prompt: What is the stressed NPV rounded to dollars?
mastery_check.worked_solution: $687.91, or +$688. Break-even annual CF ≈$5,298.52, a roughly 18.48% decline from original.

options.label: Invest: positive NPV
options.effect: Correct on the simplified risk-adjusted known scenario, subject to liquidity and uncertainties.

options.label: Reject because inflows declined
options.effect: Incorrect: decline alone does not imply negative NPV.

options.label: Ignore the sensitivity
options.effect: Fails to compare expected value with downside conditions.

bonus_challenges.feedback_for_wrong_answers: A positive NPV does not eliminate risk; present stress tests, risk tolerance, and liquidity separately.
